 Podcast 2 Chainz Defends Celebrity Perks – Keith Lee Stands Up for Regular Customers | WATCH the Debate
 A disagreement over an Atlanta restaurant review sparks a bigger question: Should celebrity status determine how customers are treated? 
 Fisher Jack • November 2, 2026 
 Add EUR on Google
 Facebook Tweet Email 
 Den of Kings podcast (Featuring 2 Chainz Kirk Franklin Keith Lee) – screenshot 
 * 2 Chainz and food critic Keith Lee are serving up a debate over celebrity privileges, restaurant service and what happens when regular folks don’t get the VIP treatment.
 Ad

 0:00 / 0:00 
 The disagreement unfolded on Kirk Franklin ‘s “ Den of Kings ” podcast where the Atlanta rapper revisited Lee’s negative review of one of his restaurants.
 What began as a discussion about food quickly turned into a conversation about fame, success and special treatment.
 For 2 Chainz, celebrity perks are among the rewards of working hard and making it big.
 For Lee, the real question is whether everyday customers receive the same quality of service when nobody recognizes their faces.

 2 Chainz Says Celebrity Perks Come with Success
 According to AtlantaFi , 2 Chainz questioned Lee about his earlier criticism of Esco Restaurant & Tapas, formerly known as Escobar, which the rapper co-founded in Atlanta in 2016.
 Although he acknowledged Lee’s right to an opinion, 2 Chainz defended the privileges that often accompany celebrity status.
 “I’m an entertainer, and obviously we get perks that other people don’t get. That’s just period, my boy. I don’t stand in line at the airport. I don’t do none of that because I done worked my ass off to do this,” he said.
 His position was clear: Entertainers work hard to achieve success, and special treatment is one of its benefits.
 But Lee wasn’t arguing about whether celebrities deserve perks. He was explaining why those perks don’t belong in his restaurant reviews.
 Keith Lee Explains Why Regular Customers Matter
 Lee maintained that his reviews are designed to show what ordinary paying customers can expect.
 That’s why he often sends family members to order food anonymously, reducing the chances that restaurants will recognize him and change their service.
 His approach has exposed situations where relatives encountered delays or restrictions that disappeared once employees recognized the popular food critic.
 For Lee, a celebrity receiving immediate attention doesn’t necessarily mean the restaurant delivers the same experience to everyone else.
 During the discussion, 2 Chainz also questioned whether Lee’s background as a former mixed martial arts fighter and his dietary habits influence his food judgments.
 Lee’s larger point remained focused on fairness and the reliability of customer reviews.
 Keith Lee – screenshot 
 Keith Lee’s Atlanta Restaurant Controversy Resurfaces
 The exchange revisits Lee’s controversial 2023 Atlanta restaurant tour, which generated national attention.
 As CNN reported , Lee encountered restaurants where his family struggled to obtain service, only for employees to offer him preferential treatment after recognizing him.
 At one establishment, he declined an opportunity to bypass waiting customers.
 The incidents sparked conversations about customer service, restaurant policies and whether celebrity recognition should determine who gets served first.
 Lee’s reviews also brought attention to smaller establishments that benefited from his recommendations.
 Celebrity Privileges Versus Everyday Customer Service
 The new exchange has circulated online, reopening questions about the relationship between fame and customer treatment.
 The disagreement highlights two different perspectives.
 2 Chainz sees VIP privileges as benefits earned through professional success.
 Lee wants his audience to understand what happens when an ordinary customer enters a restaurant without celebrity status.
 Those positions aren’t necessarily mutually exclusive. A restaurant can recognize a famous guest while still treating other paying customers fairly.
 But when the person reviewing the restaurant gets special treatment, how useful is that review to everyone else?
 Because the average diner isn’t arriving with a platinum album, millions of followers or somebody rushing to clear a table.
